subject: Mathematics
title: Amir's Race: Time and Speed
hook: Amir enters a village race, and discovers that time, distance, and speed are connected by math.

characters.name: Coach Raj
characters.role: village sports trainer, uses math to teach running

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: Amir's cousin, keeps track of times

slides.title: Racing Seconds
slides.storyContext: The village announces a 400-meter race. Amir trains with Coach Raj, who explains: 'To win, you need to run 400 meters in the shortest time. But time and speed are connected — understanding this math will help you run faster.'

slides.title: Training Day
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj times Amir running 100 meters: 20 seconds. 'Good!' says Coach. 'Now I'll teach you about speed. Speed is distance divided by time. You ran 100 meters in 20 seconds, so your speed is 100 ÷ 20 = 5 meters per second.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Speed tells you how fast something moves. It's distance traveled divided by time taken. If you run 100 meters in 20 seconds, your speed is 5 meters per second.

slides.title: What is Time?
slides.storyContext: Meera asks Amir, 'How do you know you ran for exactly 20 seconds?' Coach Raj pulls out a stopwatch. 'Time is how long something takes. We measure it in seconds, minutes, and hours. A second is very short — almost one heartbeat. A minute has 60 heartbeats.'

points.label: Time Units
points.text: Second (s) is the smallest unit we use in races. It measures very short events. A minute (min) = 60 seconds. An hour (h) = 60 minutes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Time measures how long something takes. Seconds are for short events like races. Minutes and hours are for longer things.

slides.title: Understanding Time: Seconds, Minutes, Hours
slides.storyContext: Meera keeps a stopwatch. 'One minute is 60 seconds,' she explains. 'One hour is 60 minutes, so 3,600 seconds.' Amir practices: 20 seconds, 45 seconds, 1 minute 15 seconds (= 75 seconds).

points.label: Time Conversions
points.text: 60 seconds = 1 minute. 60 minutes = 1 hour. 1 hour = 3,600 seconds. To convert: multiply to go to smaller units (minutes to seconds), divide to go to larger units (seconds to minutes).

example.problem: Convert 2 minutes 30 seconds to just seconds. Convert 180 seconds to minutes.
example.solution: 2 min 30 sec = (2 × 60) + 30 = 120 + 30 = 150 seconds. 180 seconds ÷ 60 = 3 minutes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply by 60 to convert minutes to seconds. Divide by 60 to convert seconds to minutes.

slides.title: Amir's First Real Race
slides.storyContext: In the first practice race, Amir runs 200 meters in 40 seconds. Coach Raj shouts encouragement: 'That's 5 meters per second! Your body is fast, but your mind needs to understand the math behind it. Every second counts!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Every race tells a story in numbers. Time, distance, and speed together show how well you ran.

slides.title: Measuring Distance
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj marks the track: '100 meters is about the length of the main street. 400 meters is one lap around our field. 1 kilometer is 1,000 meters — that's the distance from the village to the neighboring town.'

points.label: Distance Units
points.text: 1 kilometer (km) = 1,000 meters (m). 1 meter (m) = 100 centimeters (cm). In a race, we measure distances in meters and kilometers.

example.problem: A race is 2 kilometers long. How many meters?

slides.inSimpleWords: 1 km = 1,000 m. Use this conversion to switch between kilometers and meters.

slides.title: The Mistake That Taught a Lesson
slides.storyContext: Amir tries to run 100 meters in 15 seconds but gets tired at 80 meters. Meera checks: '80 meters in 15 seconds? That's slower than before.' Coach Raj says: 'Amir, look — when you're tired, your speed drops. Speed isn't just about running hard; it's about running smart and steady.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Pace matters. Steady running at one speed is better than starting fast and getting tired.

slides.title: Speed = Distance ÷ Time
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj teaches the formula. 'Speed equals distance divided by time. If Amir runs 400 meters in 80 seconds, his speed is 400 ÷ 80 = 5 meters per second.' Amir practices: 100 m in 20 sec → 5 m/s. 200 m in 50 sec → 4 m/s.

points.label: Speed Formula
points.text: Speed = Distance ÷ Time. If speed is S, distance is D, and time is T, then S = D ÷ T. Units: meters per second (m/s), kilometers per hour (km/h), etc.

example.problem: A runner covers 200 meters in 40 seconds. What is the speed?
example.solution: Speed = 200 m ÷ 40 s = 5 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed = how far ÷ how long. A runner who covers 100 m in 20 s has a speed of 5 m per second.

slides.title: Rearranging the Formula: Finding Time or Distance
slides.storyContext: Coach challenges Amir differently: 'If you want to run 400 meters at 5 m/s, how long will it take?' Amir rearranges: Time = Distance ÷ Speed = 400 ÷ 5 = 80 seconds. Later: 'If you have 60 seconds and want to run at 6 m/s, how far will you go?' Distance = Speed × Time = 6 × 60 = 360 meters.

points.label: Rearranging Speed Formula
points.text: Distance = Speed × Time, or D = S × T. Time = Distance ÷ Speed, or T = D ÷ S.

example.problem: Amir runs at 5 m/s. How far does he run in 25 seconds? How long to run 500 meters?
example.solution: Distance: 5 × 25 = 125 meters. Time: 500 ÷ 5 = 100 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed × Time = Distance. Distance ÷ Speed = Time. Distance ÷ Time = Speed. Know any two, find the third.

slides.title: Comparing Two Training Sessions
slides.storyContext: Monday: Amir runs 100 meters in 20 seconds. Wednesday: Amir runs 100 meters in 18 seconds. 'Coach, I'm getting faster!' Meera calculates both speeds: Monday = 5 m/s, Wednesday = 5.56 m/s. Coach nods: 'Yes, and in the big race you'll want to sustain that speed for the whole 400 meters.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Comparing speeds helps us see if we're improving. Recording times and distances lets us track progress.

slides.title: Comparing Speeds
slides.storyContext: Two runners compete: Amir (400 m in 80 s) and his friend Ravi (400 m in 100 s). Meera calculates: Amir's speed = 400 ÷ 80 = 5 m/s. Ravi's speed = 400 ÷ 100 = 4 m/s. 'Amir is faster!'

points.label: Comparing Speeds
points.text: Calculate speed for each runner or vehicle. The higher speed means faster movement. Use the same units to compare fairly.

example.problem: Runner A: 200 m in 40 s. Runner B: 300 m in 60 s. Who is faster?
example.solution: Runner A speed: 200 ÷ 40 = 5 m/s. Runner B speed: 300 ÷ 60 = 5 m/s. Same speed! It's a tie.

slides.inSimpleWords: Calculate each runner's speed, then compare. Bigger speed = faster runner.

slides.title: The Training Log
slides.storyContext: Over two weeks, Amir keeps a log of every run. Meera enters them into a table: Date, Distance, Time, Speed. By the second week, Amir's speed has improved from 5 m/s to 5.5 m/s on average. 'Hard work is paying off,' Coach Raj says, reviewing the data.
slides.inSimpleWords: Recording data helps you see if your training is working. Numbers tell the real story.

slides.title: The Big Race Day
slides.storyContext: Race day arrives. Amir runs 400 meters in 80 seconds, averaging 5 m/s. Ravi takes 100 seconds (4 m/s). A cyclist passes them both, covering 600 meters in 60 seconds (10 m/s). Meera records all speeds and times.

example.problem: In the race: Amir (400 m, 80 s), Ravi (400 m, 100 s), Cyclist (600 m, 60 s). Find each one's speed. Who is fastest? If the cyclist had run 1 hour at that speed, how far would go?
example.solution: Amir: 5 m/s. Ravi: 4 m/s. Cyclist: 10 m/s. Cyclist is fastest. In 1 hour (3,600 s): 10 × 3,600 = 36,000 meters = 36 km.

slides.inSimpleWords: Calculate each speed, compare, and use speed to predict distance over longer times.

slides.title: Amir Wins!
slides.storyContext: Amir crosses the finish line first with a time of 78 seconds for 400 meters. The crowd cheers. Meera shouts: 'That's 5.13 m/s!' Coach Raj puts a hand on Amir's shoulder: 'You understood the math, trained smart, and it paid off. This is what happens when you combine effort with knowledge.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Speed and math are tools that help athletes succeed. Training with purpose beats training without thought.

slides.title: Your Turn: Plan the Training
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj asks Amir: 'If you improve to 6 m/s for the 400-meter race, what will your time be? And if I want you to run 1 kilometer at 5 m/s, how many seconds will that take?'

example.problem: At 6 m/s for 400 m, find time. At 5 m/s for 1 km (1,000 m), find time.
example.solution: Time for 400 m at 6 m/s: 400 ÷ 6 ≈ 66.7 seconds. Time for 1,000 m at 5 m/s: 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200 seconds = 3 minutes 20 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use Time = Distance ÷ Speed to find how long a run takes.

slides.title: Speed in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Amir watches cars on the highway. 'Coach, cars go 80 kilometers per hour. That's fast! Much faster than I run.' Coach Raj nods: 'Yes, but the formula is the same: Speed = Distance ÷ Time. Whether it's you running, a car driving, or a bird flying, the math is identical.'

slides.title: Converting Speed Units
slides.storyContext: Meera asks: 'Amir runs at 5 m/s. How many kilometers per hour is that?' Coach Raj explains: 'First, convert meters to kilometers: 5 m = 0.005 km. Then, one hour = 3,600 seconds. So in one hour, he'd run: 0.005 × 3,600 = 18 km per hour.'

points.label: Converting Speed Units
points.text: 1 km = 1,000 m. 1 hour = 3,600 seconds. Speed in m/s × 3.6 = Speed in km/h.

example.problem: A car travels at 20 m/s. What is its speed in km/h?

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply m/s by 3.6 to convert to km/h. Multiply km/h by 3.6 to convert to m/s.

slides.title: The Next Race Challenge
slides.storyContext: The next village race is 800 meters. Amir wants to run it in under 160 seconds. 'What speed do I need?' Amir asks Coach Raj. Coach smiles: 'Figure it out using your formula.'

example.problem: To run 800 m in under 160 seconds, what minimum speed is needed?
example.solution: Speed = 800 ÷ 160 = 5 m/s. To run faster than 5 m/s, Amir needs a speed of at least 5.01 m/s or higher.

slides.inSimpleWords: Working backward from a goal time helps you set speed targets for training.

slides.title: Variable Speed in Real Races
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj tells Amir: 'In my day, I raced at 6 m/s for the first 100 meters, then slowed to 4.5 m/s as I got tired. By the end, I averaged 5.2 m/s.' Amir realizes: 'So runners don't always run at the same speed. The average is what matters for comparing overall performance.'

slides.title: Average Speed vs. Constant Speed
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Amir two scenarios: Scenario A: Run 100m at 5 m/s, then 100m at 4 m/s. Scenario B: Run 200m at 4.5 m/s the whole time. Which takes longer? A: 20 + 25 = 45 seconds. B: 200 ÷ 4.5 ≈ 44 seconds. 'Constant speed is slightly faster, and it's easier to sustain!'

points.label: Average Speed vs. Constant Speed
points.text: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. Constant speed is the same throughout. For the same average, constant speed often takes less total time.

example.problem: Run 300m: first 150m at 5 m/s, next 150m at 4 m/s. What's average speed?
example.solution: Time for first 150: 150 ÷ 5 = 30s. Time for next 150: 150 ÷ 4 = 37.5s. Total: 67.5s. Average: 300 ÷ 67.5 ≈ 4.4 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: Average speed is calculated using total distance and total time. It smooths out variations in pace.

slides.title: A Real-World Problem
slides.storyContext: Meera's school bus travels 15 km to school. If it takes 20 minutes (1/3 hour), what is the average speed? Meera calculates: 15 km ÷ (20/60) hours = 15 km ÷ 0.333 hours ≈ 45 km/h. 'That's the average speed of the bus!'

example.problem: A cyclist travels 24 km in 2 hours. What is the average speed?
example.solution: Speed = 24 km ÷ 2 hours = 12 km/h.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance ÷ Time always gives speed, no matter what units you use.

slides.title: The Day Amir Broke His Personal Record
slides.storyContext: After two months of training using the speed formula, Amir finally runs 400m in 75 seconds, averaging 5.33 m/s. Coach Raj says: 'You improved by breaking the task into smaller, measurable pieces. That's what math in sports is all about — measuring, analyzing, improving.'

slides.title: Graphing Speed Over Time
slides.storyContext: Meera creates a line graph showing Amir's speed improvement over weeks. Week 1: 4.8 m/s. Week 2: 4.9 m/s. Week 3: 5.0 m/s. Week 4: 5.1 m/s. The upward trend is clear. 'Visualization helps see progress at a glance!' says Meera.
slides.inSimpleWords: Line graphs show trends over time. Upward slopes show improvement.

slides.title: Acceleration vs. Constant Speed
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj teaches the concept of acceleration: 'If Amir accelerates from 4 m/s to 6 m/s over 20 seconds, his acceleration is 0.1 m/s per second. Sprinters need strong acceleration!' Amir asks: 'How do I calculate my acceleration rate?'

slides.title: The Final Lesson
slides.storyContext: As the racing season ends, Coach Raj gathers his athletes: 'Remember, speed is just one part of running. Consistency, training, strategy, and mental strength all matter. But without the math to measure progress, we're running blind. Numbers guide improvement.'

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: After the race, Amir sits with Coach Raj. 'I never knew math was the key to running fast,' Amir says. Coach smiles: 'Everything has math in it — racing, cooking, building, traveling.'

points.text: Time conversions: 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour.
Distance units: 1 km = 1,000 m. Measure distance in meters and kilometers.
Speed = Distance ÷ Time. A runner's speed is how far they go per unit time.
Distance = Speed × Time. Time = Distance ÷ Speed. Use these formulas to solve problems.
Compare speeds by calculating each one and seeing which is larger.
Record data over time to track improvement and set realistic goals.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed, distance, and time are connected. Know any two, and you can find the third.

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera's Animal Jumps: Data, Graphs, and Measurement
hook: Meera studies how far different animals can jump and organizes the data into tables and graphs.

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: curious scientist who loves animals and collecting data

characters.name: Grandfather
characters.role: patient elder with encyclopedic knowledge of village animals

slides.title: Animal Jumps
slides.storyContext: Meera watches rabbits, frogs, grasshoppers, and dogs jumping in the village courtyard. 'How far can each one jump?' she wonders. She decides to measure and collect data to find out.

slides.title: Collecting Measurements
slides.storyContext: Meera marks a starting line with chalk and measures how far each animal jumps using a meter stick. Amir writes down the numbers: Rabbit 1: 2 m, Rabbit 2: 1.8 m, Frog 1: 0.6 m, Frog 2: 0.7 m, Grasshopper 1: 0.5 m, Grasshopper 2: 0.4 m, Dog 1: 1.5 m, Dog 2: 1.2 m. 'Now we organize this data,' says Meera.
slides.inSimpleWords: Data is information we collect by measuring or observing. We organize data into tables to see patterns.

slides.title: Meera's Question
slides.storyContext: Amir asks: 'Meera, why do you care how far these animals jump?' Meera replies: 'Different animals are built differently. A rabbit has strong back legs. A frog is built for jumping. By collecting data, I can see which animals are the best jumpers and understand nature better.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Data helps us ask and answer questions about the world. Comparing measurements shows differences and patterns.

slides.title: Measuring in Meters and Centimeters
slides.storyContext: Meera's rabbit jumps 2 meters. Another jumps 1 meter 80 centimeters (1.8 m). Grandfather explains: '1 meter = 100 centimeters. So 1 meter 80 centimeters is 180 centimeters total, or 1.8 meters.'

points.label: Meter-Centimeter Conversion
points.text: 1 meter = 100 centimeters. To convert meters to centimeters, multiply by 100. To convert centimeters to meters, divide by 100.

example.problem: A frog jumps 65 centimeters. Express this in meters.
example.solution: 65 cm ÷ 100 = 0.65 meters (or 65 cm = 0 m 65 cm).

slides.inSimpleWords: 1 meter = 100 cm. 1.5 meters = 150 cm. 80 cm = 0.8 meters.

image.alt: Measuring in Meters and Centimeters — Animal Jumps

slides.title: Converting Measurements
slides.storyContext: Some measurements were in centimeters, some in meters. Amir says: 'Let's convert everything to meters for consistency.' Meera converts: 60 cm = 0.6 m, 70 cm = 0.7 m, 50 cm = 0.5 m, 40 cm = 0.4 m. 'Now all our data is in the same units!'
slides.inSimpleWords: To compare measurements fairly, convert them to the same unit first.

slides.title: Creating a Data Table
slides.storyContext: Meera organizes the jump data into a clear table: Animal type, Number of jumps recorded, Average jump distance. Rabbit: 2, 1.9 m. Frog: 2, 0.65 m. Grasshopper: 2, 0.45 m. Dog: 2, 1.35 m. 'Now we can see which animal jumps farthest!'

points.label: Organizing Data in Tables
points.text: A table lists data in rows and columns. Rows are categories (animal type). Columns are measurements (distance, frequency, etc.). This makes it easy to compare and analyze.

example.problem: Create a table for: Rabbit 2 m, 1.8 m; Frog 0.6 m, 0.7 m. Calculate averages.
example.solution: Rabbit average: (2 + 1.8) ÷ 2 = 1.9 m. Frog average: (0.6 + 0.7) ÷ 2 = 0.65 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: A table organizes data so you can see patterns. Rows and columns make data easy to read and compare.

slides.title: Looking for Patterns
slides.storyContext: Meera points to the table: 'Look, Amir! All rabbits jump around 1.8-2 meters. All frogs jump around 0.6-0.7 meters. There's a pattern — each animal type has its own jumping range.'
slides.inSimpleWords: When you organize data, patterns become clear. Data tells stories about nature.

slides.title: Calculating Averages (Mean)
slides.storyContext: Meera has three grasshopper jump measurements: 0.5 m, 0.4 m, and 0.6 m. 'What's the average jump?' Amir adds: 0.5 + 0.4 + 0.6 = 1.5 m. Then divides by 3: 1.5 ÷ 3 = 0.5 m average.

points.label: Calculating the Mean (Average)
points.text: Add all the values, then divide by how many values there are. Average = (sum of all values) ÷ (number of values).

example.problem: Dog jumps: 1.5 m, 1.2 m, 1.4 m. What is the average?

slides.inSimpleWords: Average = sum of all values ÷ number of values. It tells you the typical value in a set.

slides.title: Why Averages Matter
slides.storyContext: Amir asks: 'Meera, why do we need the average? We already have each jump distance.' Meera explains: 'The average tells us what's typical for each animal. One jump might be a lucky jump, but the average represents the animal's real ability.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Average is the typical or middle value. It smooths out lucky or unlucky jumps.

slides.title: Creating a Bar Graph
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a bar graph on graph paper. The x-axis lists animals (Rabbit, Frog, Grasshopper, Dog). The y-axis shows distance in meters (0 to 2 m). She draws bars for each animal's average jump. The rabbit bar is tallest, the grasshopper bar shortest.

points.label: Bar Graphs
points.text: A bar graph uses rectangular bars to show data. The height of each bar represents a value. Bar graphs make it easy to compare values at a glance.

example.problem: Draw a bar graph for: Rabbit 1.9 m, Frog 0.65 m, Grasshopper 0.45 m, Dog 1.35 m.
example.solution: Create axes. X-axis: animal names. Y-axis: distance (0-2 m). Draw bars: Rabbit tallest, then Dog, then Frog, then Grasshopper.

slides.inSimpleWords: In a bar graph, taller bars mean bigger values. You can compare all values at once by looking at bar heights.

slides.title: The Moment of Clarity
slides.storyContext: As Meera finishes drawing the bar graph, she gasps: 'Look how clear this is now! Without the graph, I had to read the table carefully. But with the graph, I can see at a glance that rabbits are the best jumpers and grasshoppers jump the shortest distances.' Amir agrees: 'A picture really does say a thousand words!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Graphs turn numbers into pictures that our brains can understand quickly.

slides.title: Reading and Interpreting Graphs
slides.storyContext: Looking at the bar graph, Meera asks: 'Which animal jumps the farthest? How much farther does a rabbit jump than a frog?' Amir reads: 'Rabbit jumps 1.9 m, frog jumps 0.65 m. Difference: 1.9 - 0.65 = 1.25 m.'

points.label: Analyzing Graphs
points.text: Read the axes carefully. Compare bar heights. Calculate differences and ratios if needed. Look for trends (is data increasing, decreasing, or stable?).

example.problem: From the bar graph: How much farther does a dog jump than a grasshopper?
example.solution: Dog: 1.35 m. Grasshopper: 0.45 m. Difference: 1.35 - 0.45 = 0.9 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Read a graph by looking at the axes and comparing bar heights. You can calculate differences between values.

slides.title: Grandfather's Observation
slides.storyContext: Grandfather looks at Meera's graph and says: 'Interesting! Rabbits and dogs are similar in size, but rabbits jump about 40 percent farther. And frogs, though smaller, jump nearly half the distance of a dog. Each animal is optimized for its own needs.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Graphs and data help us understand how nature works and why different animals behave differently.

slides.title: The Complete Study
slides.storyContext: Meera writes a report: 'I measured jump distances for 4 animals. Rabbits jump the farthest (average 1.9 m), followed by dogs (1.35 m), frogs (0.65 m), and grasshoppers (0.45 m). I organized the data in a table and created a bar graph to show the comparison.'

example.problem: Create a full report: table, average calculations, and graph interpretation.
example.solution:
Table:
Animal | Jump 1 | Jump 2 | Average
Rabbit | 2.0 | 1.8 | 1.9
Frog | 0.6 | 0.7 | 0.65
Grasshopper | 0.5 | 0.4 | 0.45
Dog | 1.5 | 1.2 | 1.35

Interpretation: Rabbit jumps farthest; grasshopper jumps shortest.

slides.inSimpleWords: A complete data analysis includes measurements, a table, averages, a graph, and conclusions.

slides.title: Presenting at the Fair
slides.storyContext: At the village fair, Meera displays her poster with the data, table, graph, and a small demonstration with pictures of each animal. Children gather around, fascinated. 'Wow, rabbits jump that far?' says one child. Meera smiles proudly. 'Yes, and now you can see it clearly in the graph.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Good data presentation helps others learn and understand your findings.

slides.title: Your Turn: Analyze More Animals
slides.storyContext: Grandfather asks Meera: 'If a cat jumps 1.1 m and 1.3 m, what's its average? Where does it fit in your graph? Which animals jump twice as far as a grasshopper?'

example.problem: Cat jumps: 1.1 m, 1.3 m. Find average. Is it more or less than a dog's average (1.35 m)? Which animal jumps about 2× a grasshopper's distance (0.45 m)?
example.solution: Cat average: (1.1 + 1.3) ÷ 2 = 1.2 m. Less than dog's 1.35 m. 2 × grasshopper: 2 × 0.45 = 0.9 m ≈ dog's distance (1.35 m is close, but not exactly 2×; frog at 0.65 m is not 2×; rabbit at 1.9 m is 4.2×).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use averages and graphs to compare new data with existing data. Look for patterns and multiples.

slides.title: Finding the Median
slides.storyContext: Amir joins Meera and Grandfather. He asks: 'Is the average always the best way to describe the data?' Grandfather says: 'Good question! Sometimes the average can be misleading if there's an outlier — a value very different from the rest. The median is another useful measure.'

slides.title: Median and Mode
slides.storyContext: Meera's rabbit jumps: 2.0 m, 1.8 m, 2.1 m. Sorted: 1.8, 2.0, 2.1. 'The middle value is 2.0 m — that's the median,' explains Grandfather. 'For the mode (most common value), we look for the value that appears most often.'

points.label: Median
points.text: The middle value when data is sorted from smallest to largest. It's not affected by extreme outliers.

points.label: Mode
points.text: The value that appears most frequently in a dataset. There can be one mode or multiple modes.

example.problem: Dog jumps: 1.5 m, 1.2 m, 1.4 m, 1.5 m, 1.3 m. Find median and mode.
example.solution: Sorted: 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 1.5. Median = 1.4 m (middle value). Mode = 1.5 m (appears twice).

slides.inSimpleWords: Median is the middle value. Mode is the most common value. Both describe data differently than average.

slides.title: Comparing Data Representations
slides.storyContext: Meera compares statistics for the rabbit's jumps: Average = 1.9 m, Median = 2.0 m, Mode = none (no repeat). 'All three tell slightly different stories about the same data!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Average, median, and mode each give different insight into what the data represents.

slides.title: Range and Spread of Data
slides.storyContext: Grandfather points: 'Look at the rabbit's range: highest 2.0 m, lowest 1.8 m, so the range is 0.2 m. The frog's range: 0.7 - 0.6 = 0.1 m. Rabbits have more variable jumps; frogs are more consistent.'

points.label: Range
points.text: Highest value minus lowest value. It shows how spread out the data is.

points.label: Consistency
points.text: A smaller range means more consistent performance; a larger range means more variability.

example.problem: Grasshopper jumps: 0.5 m, 0.4 m, 0.6 m. Find the range.

slides.inSimpleWords: Range tells you how much the values differ from each other. Smaller range = more consistent.

slides.title: Comparing Jump Consistency
slides.storyContext: Meera notices: 'Rabbits have jumps ranging from 1.8 to 2.0 meters. Frogs range from 0.6 to 0.7 meters. Which is more consistent?' Amir calculates ranges: Rabbit range = 0.2m, Frog range = 0.1m. 'Frogs are more consistent jumpers!' says Meera, amazed at what the data shows.

slides.title: Comparing Multiple Variables
slides.storyContext: Grandfather suggests: 'Now that you know the distance each animal jumps, measure how long each jump takes. Then you can calculate speed!' Meera realizes: 'A frog that jumps 0.7m in 0.5 seconds is faster than it seems!'

slides.title: The Surprising Discovery
slides.storyContext: After calculating jump speeds, Meera discovers that frogs have the fastest jumping speed relative to their body size! 'This teaches me something important,' she tells Grandfather. 'Data doesn't lie. Sometimes what looks slower is actually faster when you measure it properly.'

slides.title: Deeper Analysis with Data
slides.storyContext: Meera creates a new analysis: comparing jump distance to jump speed. She finds that while rabbits jump farthest, frogs jump with greater acceleration. 'Each animal is optimized for its own lifestyle,' she concludes.

slides.title: Design Your Own Experiment
slides.storyContext: Meera decides to measure how high each animal can jump vertically instead of horizontally. 'I can use the same methods: measure, organize data, calculate averages, and create a graph. I wonder if the ranking will be the same?'

example.problem: Design an experiment plan: What measurements would you take? How would you organize and display the data?
example.solution: Measure vertical jump height (from ground to highest point each animal reaches). Use same 4 animals. Record 2-3 jumps each. Create table with Animal, Jump 1 (cm), Jump 2 (cm), Jump 3 (cm), Average (cm). Convert to meters if needed. Create bar graph comparing vertical jump heights.

slides.inSimpleWords: The same data analysis methods can be used for different types of measurements and experiments.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Meera displays her poster with the data, graph, and conclusions at the village school fair. Grandfather smiles: 'You've learned to collect data, organize it, and tell a story with numbers and graphs.'

points.text: Measurement: use meters and centimeters; 1 m = 100 cm.
Data tables organize information in rows and columns for easy comparison.
Average (mean) = sum of values ÷ number of values. It represents a typical value.
Bar graphs use bar height to show values visually. Easy to compare at a glance.
Read graphs by checking axes, comparing heights, and calculating differences.
Data analysis tells stories about the world. Measurement, organization, and graphs reveal patterns.

slides.inSimpleWords: Data, tables, and graphs help us understand the world. Measurements, organization, and analysis tell stories.

subject: Mathematics
title: Raj and Priya's Village Map Adventure
hook: Help Raj and Priya find their way around the village using maps and directions.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Raj's clever cousin with a compass

slides.title: Maps and Locations
slides.storyContext: Raj and Priya arrive at their grandmother's village for summer holidays. Dadi pulls out an old hand-drawn map of the village and asks them to help find the local temple for evening prayers.
slides.inSimpleWords: A map is a picture that shows where things are in a place.

image.alt: Maps and Locations — Maps and Locations

slides.title: The Mystery of Dadi's Map
slides.storyContext: Dadi shows them her hand-drawn village map with the school, temple, marketplace, well, and her house marked. Raj gets excited: 'But Dadi, how do we know which way is north?' Priya pulls out a small compass from her pocket. Together, they realize the map has a compass rose drawn in the corner showing North, South, East, and West.
slides.inSimpleWords: Maps use directions like North, South, East, and West to show us how to get places.

image.alt: The Mystery of Dadi's Map — Maps and Locations

slides.title: Learning from a Compass
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'A compass always points to magnetic north. If I hold it still, the needle points that way.' She holds the compass in the sun. 'And we know that the sun rises in the east and sets in the west. So we can figure out all four directions from any one direction we know.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A compass is a tool that helps you find directions. It always points north.

slides.title: Directions: The Four Cardinal Points
slides.storyContext: Standing in the middle of the village square, Dadi points: 'North is where the mountains are, South toward the river, East toward the sunrise, West toward the sunset.' Raj repeats the directions: North-East-South-West, and Priya adds, 'And we can remember it as NEWS!'

points.label: Cardinal Directions
points.text: North (N) = up, South (S) = down, East (E) = right (sunrise), West (W) = left (sunset)

points.label: Compass Rose
points.text: A symbol on the map showing these four directions

points.label: Finding your way
points.text: Always look for the compass rose to know which way to go

example.problem: If you are at Dadi's house facing the temple which is to the North, where would you turn to face the marketplace which is to the East?
example.solution: You would turn 90° to your right (clockwise) to face East.

slides.inSimpleWords: Directions help us know which way to go: North is up, South is down, East is right, West is left.

image.alt: Directions: The Four Cardinal Points — Maps and Locations

slides.title: Intermediate Directions
slides.storyContext: Raj asks: 'Dadi, what if something isn't exactly North or exactly East? It's sort of in between?' Dadi smiles: 'Excellent question! Between North and East is Northeast. Between South and West is Southwest. We have eight main directions on a full compass rose.' Priya draws them on the map.
slides.inSimpleWords: Between the four main directions are four more: Northeast, Northwest, Southeast, Southwest.

slides.title: Grid Lines: Making a Square Map
slides.storyContext: Priya draws a grid on Dadi's map using a ruler. 'Now we can find any place using rows and columns, like a checkerboard!' Each square in the grid is labeled. Dadi's house is in the square at Column B, Row 2. Raj picks a red crayon and marks it.

points.label: Grid
points.text: A pattern of lines that form squares on a map

points.label: Rows
points.text: Horizontal lines numbered from bottom (1) to top (for vertical position)

points.label: Columns
points.text: Vertical lines labeled A, B, C, D... from left to right (for horizontal position)

points.label: Grid Reference
points.text: Combining column letter and row number tells you exactly where something is

example.problem: The well is at column D, row 3. The school is at column B, row 4. Describe their positions on the grid.
example.solution: Well is in column D (4th column from left), row 3 (3rd row from bottom). School is in column B (2nd column from left), row 4 (4th row from bottom).

slides.inSimpleWords: A grid is like a checkerboard on the map. We use letters for columns and numbers for rows to pinpoint any location.

image.alt: Grid Lines: Making a Square Map — Maps and Locations

slides.title: Finding the Temple
slides.storyContext: Looking at the grid, Priya reads: 'Dadi's house is at B2. The temple is at D4. That's two columns to the right and two rows up.' Raj traces with his finger: 'So we go northeast from the house to reach the temple. The grid makes it so easy!'
slides.inSimpleWords: A grid reference tells you exactly where to go. You can trace a path on the map.

slides.title: Scale: Measuring Real Distances
slides.storyContext: Raj asks: 'Dadi, if the temple is just 1 cm away on your map, how far is it to really walk there?' Dadi smiles and points to the corner of her map: 'See this line marked 1 cm = 100 meters? That's the scale. So 1 cm on my map is 100 meters in real life.'

points.label: Map Scale
points.text: A ratio showing how map distance relates to real-world distance

points.label: Example scales
points.text: 1 cm = 100 m (small village), 1 cm = 1 km (larger area), 1 inch = 1 mile (very large areas)

points.label: Using scale
points.text: Measure the distance on the map, then multiply by the scale to find the real distance

example.problem: On Dadi's map, the distance from school to the marketplace is 3 cm. If the scale is 1 cm = 100 m, how far is it really?
example.solution: 3 cm × 100 m per cm = 300 meters in real life.

slides.inSimpleWords: Scale tells us how big real things actually are compared to the map. A small line on the map might mean a long walk in real life.

slides.title: Using the Scale to Plan a Walk
slides.storyContext: Priya measures on the map with a ruler: 'The distance from Dadi's house to the marketplace is about 2.5 cm.' Using the scale of 1 cm = 100 m, she calculates: '2.5 × 100 = 250 meters. That's about a 5-minute walk!' Dadi nods approvingly.
slides.inSimpleWords: With the scale, you can figure out how long a journey will take before you start walking.

slides.title: Symbols on Maps: A Secret Code
slides.storyContext: Priya flips to the back of Dadi's map and finds a legend: a small temple symbol ⛩️, a school symbol 🏫, a house symbol 🏠, and a tree symbol 🌳. 'Dadi, this is like a secret code! Each symbol means something different,' she exclaims. Dadi nods: 'Yes, without the legend, we wouldn't know what we're looking at.'

points.label: Map Legend
points.text: A key that explains what each symbol or color on the map means

points.label: Common symbols
points.text: Houses (small squares), schools (flag), temples (spire), trees (green dots), rivers (blue wavy lines)

points.label: Why symbols?
points.text: Drawing real pictures would make the map too crowded; symbols are simple and clear

example.problem: On a map legend, you see: ⛩️ = temple, 🏥 = health center, 💧 = well. If there are 3 wells marked on the map, how many sources of water does the village have?
example.solution: At least 3, though there may be more wells not marked on the map.

slides.inSimpleWords: Map symbols are like a picture code. A legend tells you what each symbol means.

slides.title: Decoding the Legend
slides.storyContext: Raj plays detective. Using the legend, he identifies all the important locations on Dadi's map: three temples, two schools, a marketplace, a well, a health center, and many houses. 'This map shows everything important in the village!' he exclaims.
slides.inSimpleWords: A legend is your key to understanding everything on a map.

slides.title: Different Types of Maps
slides.storyContext: At Dadi's house, Raj finds three different maps in a drawer: a hand-drawn village map (physical features like rivers and trees), a road map with marked routes, and a thematic map showing where crops grow. 'Which one is best?' he asks. Priya says, 'They show different things! We choose based on what we need to find.'

points.label: Physical Maps
points.text: Show natural features: rivers, mountains, forests, valleys

points.label: Political Maps
points.text: Show borders, states, cities, countries

points.label: Road/Street Maps
points.text: Show streets, highways, landmarks for navigation

points.label: Thematic Maps
points.text: Show specific information like weather, population, or crop distribution

slides.inSimpleWords: Different maps show different information. Pick the right map for what you want to find out.

slides.title: Choosing the Right Map
slides.storyContext: Priya wants to find all the fields where sugarcane grows. 'The thematic map is perfect for this!' The physical map shows rivers and mountains, but not crops. The road map shows streets but not agriculture. 'Each map tells a different story,' says Dadi.
slides.inSimpleWords: Different maps answer different questions. Choose the map that shows what you need.

slides.title: Reading Dadi's Village Map: A Full Task
slides.storyContext: Now Raj and Priya are ready for the real challenge. Dadi hands them the village map and asks them to plan a route from her house to the marketplace, passing by the school. They use the grid references, cardinal directions, and the scale to plan their walk.

example.problem: Using the village map (scale: 1 cm = 100 m, grid shown), Dadi's house is at B2, the school is at C3, and the marketplace is at D2. Plan a route and calculate the total walking distance. Which direction from school leads to the marketplace?
example.solution: Route: Start at B2 (Dadi's house) → go East and North to C3 (school) → then go East and South to D2 (marketplace). Direction from school to market: East and South (Southeast). Distance: approximately 2.5 cm on map = 250 meters in real life.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reading a map means using the grid, directions, and scale together to find places and measure distances.

slides.title: Can You Find the Hidden Well?
slides.storyContext: Dadi gives Raj and Priya a challenge before dinner: 'There's a well hidden on the eastern edge of the village. It's 2 cm from the marketplace according to the scale. Can you find it on the map?' Raj and Priya work together, measuring, looking at the scale, and checking the compass rose.

example.problem: Starting from the marketplace at D2, go 2 cm due East (right) on a map with scale 1 cm = 100 m. What is the real distance, and approximately at which grid position should the well be?
example.solution: Real distance: 2 cm × 100 m/cm = 200 meters. The well would be approximately at E2 on the grid (one column to the right, same row).

slides.inSimpleWords: Using a map, you can find hidden places by following directions and using the scale.

slides.title: Understanding Map Distortion
slides.storyContext: Raj notices: 'Dadi, on your map, the marketplace looks farther from school in one direction than the other, but I walked between them and it felt symmetric.' Dadi smiles: 'Maps flatten a round world onto flat paper. That causes distortion. No map is perfect, but this one works for our small village.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Maps are representations, not perfect pictures. Small distortions are normal and acceptable for navigation.

slides.title: Latitude and Longitude
slides.storyContext: Priya asks about bigger maps. 'How do we locate places on a real map of India?' Dadi explains: 'Maps of entire countries and the world use lines called latitude (horizontal) and longitude (vertical). Together, they form a grid that covers the whole Earth. Every place has unique coordinates.'

points.label: Latitude
points.text: Horizontal lines running East-West. They measure distance North or South from the equator (0° to 90°).

points.label: Longitude
points.text: Vertical lines running North-South. They measure distance East or West from the Prime Meridian (0° to 180°).

points.label: Coordinates
points.text: Every place on Earth can be identified by its latitude and longitude: e.g., New Delhi is about 28.7°N, 77.2°E.

slides.inSimpleWords: Latitude and longitude are invisible lines on Earth that form a global grid. Every place has unique coordinates.

slides.title: Navigating Without a Map
slides.storyContext: Raj asks: 'What if we didn't have a map? How would we find our way?' Priya suggests: 'Use the sun, stars, and compass. The sun always rises in the East and sets in the West. At night, we can find North by the North Star.' Dadi nods approvingly: 'True navigation skills!'

slides.title: Map Skills in Technology
slides.storyContext: Priya mentions GPS: 'Modern phones have GPS that shows our exact location using coordinates and satellites. But the underlying map concepts are the same: directions, scale, symbols, and grids.' Dadi says: 'Technology has changed, but map-reading remains essential.'

points.label: GPS (Global Positioning System)
points.text: Uses satellites to determine precise location based on latitude and longitude.

points.label: Digital Maps
points.text: Show real-time information, allow zooming, and calculate routes automatically.

points.label: Skills Remain
points.text: Understanding directions, scales, and symbols helps interpret any map, digital or paper.

slides.inSimpleWords: Technology has changed maps, but the core concepts of directions, scale, and navigation remain the same.

slides.title: Raj and Priya's First Solo Adventure
slides.storyContext: The next day, Dadi gives Raj and Priya the map and a challenge: 'Go find three new places I've marked with red dots and bring me a small stone from each location.' Using all their new skills—directions, grid, scale, and symbols—they successfully complete the treasure hunt.

slides.title: Comparing Old and New Maps
slides.storyContext: Priya finds an even older map in Dadi's trunk. 'Dadi, why is the marketplace in a different location here?' Dadi smiles: 'The village changed. We built a new marketplace 100 years ago. Maps reflect the present time, not the past.'

slides.title: Teaching Others to Read Maps
slides.storyContext: Raj and Priya teach their younger cousin to read the map. 'First, find the compass rose to know which way is north. Then use the grid to pinpoint locations. Finally, use the scale to measure real distances.' The younger cousin catches on quickly!

slides.title: Relative vs. Absolute Location
slides.storyContext: Priya realizes: 'We describe the temple's location two ways: relative (North of Dadi's house, next to the marketplace) or absolute (grid position D4, or with coordinates). Both are useful!'

points.label: Relative Location
points.text: Described in relation to other places (north of, west of, between, etc.)

points.label: Absolute Location
points.text: Specific coordinates or grid references (grid D4, latitude 28.7°N, etc.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Relative location uses nearby landmarks. Absolute location uses exact coordinates or grid positions.

slides.title: Maps Are Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Priya realizes: 'Maps are not just for villages. They're on phones, websites, in books about geography, and in games. Whenever you see a bird's-eye view of a place, it's a map. The skills we learned apply everywhere!'

slides.title: Design Your Own Village Map
slides.storyContext: Dadi asks Raj and Priya: 'If you were to draw a map of this village, what features would you include? How would you draw it? What legend would you create?' The children discuss their ideas, thinking about what information is most important.

example.problem: Design a simple village map. What symbols would you use? What scale? What grid would you draw? What features must be included?
example.solution: Include: main landmarks (temple, school, marketplace, well, health center, houses), natural features (river if present, trees), a compass rose showing all 8 directions, a grid with letters and numbers, a scale (e.g., 1 cm = 100 m), and a legend explaining all symbols.

slides.inSimpleWords: Creating a map requires planning about what to include, how to show it, and how to help others read it.

slides.title: What We Learned Today
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Raj and Priya sit with Dadi, proudly holding the map. 'We found everything we needed,' says Priya. Dadi smiles: 'You learned to read a map like true explorers.'

points.label: Directions
points.text: North, South, East, West (NEWS) help us know which way to go

points.label: Grid
points.text: Columns (letters) and rows (numbers) pinpoint exact locations

points.label: Scale
points.text: Tells us how map distance relates to real distance

points.label: Symbols & Legend
points.text: A key code that explains what each symbol means

points.label: Map Types
points.text: Different maps show different information; choose the right one for your need

points.label: Compass Rose
points.text: Shows all 8 directions and helps orient the map to the real world

slides.inSimpleWords: Maps are tools that help us find our way. With directions, a grid, scale, and symbols, we can navigate anywhere.
